STOCKHOLM -- The trial of Kerstin Wahlgrenova, a former procurement officer at the regional transport authority, opened on Monday in a crowded courtroom on Kungsholmen. Prosecutors allege that she steered three contracts for tram maintenance toward a supplier owned by a distant relative.

The case has drawn attention well beyond the capital, partly because of how long it took to reach court. Auditors first flagged irregularities in the authority's accounts nearly six years ago, but the internal review stalled after two senior managers resigned and a key spreadsheet was found to have been overwritten. Journalists at a local newspaper spent months reconstructing the paper trail, filing dozens of freedom-of-information requests and interviewing former staff who said they had been discouraged from raising concerns.

Defense lawyers spent much of the first morning challenging the chain of custody for several email archives. They argued that the files had been copied onto an unencrypted laptop by a consultant who was later dismissed for unrelated reasons, and that no reliable log shows who opened them in the intervening months. The presiding judge allowed the material to be entered but said its weight would be assessed at the end of the proceedings.

Outside the building, a small group of union members held placards calling for wider reforms to how public bodies award contracts. Several said they were less interested in any single verdict than in whether the authority would finally publish its full tender records. The transport minister declined to comment, citing the ongoing case.

By the time the court adjourned on Thursday, several observers in the public gallery were saying openly that the evidence against Wahlgrenova looked far thinner than the indictment had suggested.

The Centro Studi Valdarnese Societa Cooperativa was founded in 1974 by a group of teachers and local historians in the upper Arno valley. Its original aim was modest: to collect parish registers, land deeds and oral testimonies before they were lost to damp cellars and house clearances.

In the decades after the Second World War, the valley changed faster than at almost any time in its history. Sharecropping, which had organized rural life for centuries, collapsed within a single generation. Families who had worked the same hillside plots for a dozen generations moved to the textile mills of Prato or the new industrial zones around Florence. Farmhouses were abandoned, then sold to foreign buyers, then restored in ways that often erased the evidence of how they had once been used.

Volunteers began by recording elderly residents describing the annual cycle of work: the wheat harvest, the grape picking, the slaughter of the pig in December, the careful division of produce between landlord and tenant. These recordings, made on reel-to-reel tape and later digitized, are now among the most frequently consulted sources for scholars of Tuscan rural society.

The archive also holds an unusual collection of account books kept by estate managers, some dating to the 1820s. Read alongside the oral testimony, they show how tenants negotiated, resisted and occasionally outmaneuvered the people who owned the land. Several doctoral theses have been built almost entirely on this material.

Today, researchers from as far away as Japan and Brazil arrange visits months in advance, and a growing share of the catalogue is available online through a partnership with the University of Siena, a project that the Centro Studi Valdarnese Societa Cooperativa still funds largely from members' dues.

The Halvorsen FX-40 mesh node is designed for homes and small offices that need reliable coverage across several floors. This guide covers first-time setup, placement and the most common troubleshooting steps.

Before you begin, make sure your internet service provider's modem is working and connected to the wall. Unplug any older router you plan to replace, and keep its admin password handy in case you need to copy over custom settings such as port forwarding rules or a static IP reservation.

Placement matters more than most people expect. Wireless signals weaken as they pass through concrete, brick, mirrors and large appliances, and fish tanks are notoriously bad. Aim for a central, elevated position on each floor, ideally on a shelf rather than the floor and away from microwaves or cordless phone bases. If you are using more than one unit, place secondary units roughly halfway between the primary unit and the area where coverage is weak, not inside the dead zone itself.

Once everything is plugged in, open the companion app and follow the prompts. The app will detect your connection type, ask you to name your network and choose a password, and then search for additional units. This process usually takes between five and ten minutes. Do not unplug anything while the status light is blinking amber, as interrupting a firmware update can leave a unit unresponsive.

If devices keep dropping their connection, try switching off band steering in the advanced settings and assigning older devices to the 2.4 GHz band manually. Smart plugs and some printers handle mixed-band networks poorly.

For anything not covered here, our support team can remotely check the diagnostic logs stored on your Halvorsen FX-40 unit once you grant permission in the app.

If your sourdough loaves spread flat on the baking tray, the Lindqvist double-fold technique may help. It is a gentle way of building tension in high-hydration dough without the vigorous kneading that many home bakers find tiring.

Start with a well-fed starter. It should roughly double in volume within four to six hours of feeding and smell pleasantly sour rather than sharp or like nail polish. Mix your flour and most of the water first and let the mixture rest for forty minutes; this rest, called autolyse, lets the flour absorb water and begin developing gluten on its own.

Next, add the starter and salt along with the remaining water. Squeeze the dough through your fingers until everything is evenly combined. It will feel sticky and shaggy at this stage, which is normal. Resist the urge to add more flour.

Cover the bowl and leave it somewhere warm, ideally around 24 degrees Celsius. Over the next few hours the dough will become smoother, more elastic and noticeably airier. Check it every half hour. You are looking for a domed surface, a few bubbles at the edges and a slight wobble when you shake the bowl.

Temperature is the variable that catches most people out. A cold kitchen can double the time needed, while a hot summer afternoon can push the dough past its peak before you notice. Keeping a simple thermometer next to the bowl removes much of the guesswork.

Shaping and the overnight cold proof come later. For now, wet your hands, lift one edge of the dough, stretch it upward and lay it over the centre, then turn the bowl and repeat, because this is where the Lindqvist double-fold technique actually begins.

Ottoline Brackenridge-Vasquez was born in 1891 in Valparaiso, the daughter of a Scottish shipping clerk and a Chilean schoolteacher. She would become one of the first women to publish original research on the tidal ecology of the southern Pacific coast.

Her childhood was shaped by the harbour. Her father's office overlooked the docks, and she spent long afternoons watching cargo being unloaded and listening to sailors describe ports she would not see for decades. Her mother insisted on a rigorous education at home, teaching her mathematics, French and botany long before she was allowed to attend a secondary school.

At nineteen she travelled to Edinburgh, where she enrolled in natural science classes that were only partly open to women. She was barred from some laboratory sessions and had to borrow notes from male classmates, several of whom later became lifelong correspondents. Her early letters home describe cold lodgings, long hours in the library and an increasing fascination with marine invertebrates.

The outbreak of war in 1914 interrupted her plans. She worked for three years as a hospital clerk, a period she rarely discussed in later life. When she finally returned to Chile, she took a teaching post in a girls' school and spent her holidays mapping rock pools along a remote stretch of coastline south of the city.

Her notebooks from those summers, filled with careful drawings of anemones, chitons and barnacles, were rediscovered in a university basement in 1987. Marine biologists who examined them were struck by how closely her observations anticipated work published decades later, and a new edition of the notebooks has finally restored the reputation of Brackenridge-Vasquez among historians of science.

Ranolazine is an anti-anginal agent used in the management of chronic stable angina, usually as an add-on when beta blockers, calcium channel blockers or nitrates fail to control symptoms adequately. Unlike many older anti-anginal drugs, it has little effect on heart rate or blood pressure.

Its principal mechanism is inhibition of the late sodium current in cardiac myocytes. Under ischemic conditions, this late current increases, leading to intracellular sodium accumulation and, through the sodium-calcium exchanger, calcium overload. Excess calcium impairs relaxation of the heart muscle during diastole, raising wall tension and oxygen demand. By reducing this cascade, the drug improves diastolic function and myocardial efficiency.

Oral bioavailability is variable, and the extended-release formulation is taken twice daily. Metabolism occurs primarily in the liver via CYP3A4, with a smaller contribution from CYP2D6. This has important practical consequences. Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors such as ketoconazole and clarithromycin can raise plasma concentrations substantially and are contraindicated, while moderate inhibitors such as diltiazem and verapamil require dose limitation. Inducers such as rifampicin may reduce plasma levels to the point of therapeutic failure.

The drug also inhibits P-glycoprotein and CYP2D6 to some extent, which can increase exposure to digoxin, simvastatin and certain tricyclic antidepressants. Clinicians should review the full medication list before initiating therapy, particularly in elderly patients taking several cardiovascular drugs at once.

Dose-dependent QT prolongation has been observed, although clinical trials have not shown an increase in arrhythmic events. Common adverse effects include dizziness, constipation, nausea and headache.

In patients with significant hepatic impairment, the safety of ranolazine has not been established and its use is generally avoided.

# backup_tools.py
# Utilities for creating and restoring project snapshots.
# The main entry point is snapshot_work_dir, which copies the working
# directory into a timestamped archive folder.

import os
import shutil
import time
import logging

log = logging.getLogger(__name__)

IGNORED = {'.git', '__pycache__', 'node_modules', '.venv'}


def _should_skip(name):
    # Hidden editor files and build caches are not worth archiving.
    # Keeping this check small makes it easy to extend later.
    return name in IGNORED or name.endswith('.swp')


def _copy_tree(src, dst):
    # shutil.copytree would work, but we want per-file logging and
    # the ability to skip large binaries without failing the whole run.
    for root, dirs, files in os.walk(src):
        dirs[:] = [d for d in dirs if not _should_skip(d)]
        rel = os.path.relpath(root, src)
        target = os.path.join(dst, rel)
        os.makedirs(target, exist_ok=True)
        for f in files:
            if _should_skip(f):
                continue
            s = os.path.join(root, f)
            if os.path.getsize(s) > 200_000_000:
                log.warning('skipping large file %s', s)
                continue
            shutil.copy2(s, os.path.join(target, f))


def prune_old(archive_root, keep=10):
    # Remove the oldest archives so the backup disk does not fill up.
    # Folders are named by timestamp, so a plain sort is chronological.
    entries = sorted(os.listdir(archive_root))
    for old in entries[:-keep]:
        shutil.rmtree(os.path.join(archive_root, old), ignore_errors=True)


def make_archive_path(archive_root):
    stamp = time.strftime('%Y%m%d-%H%M%S')
    return os.path.join(archive_root, stamp)


# NOTE: callers should run prune_old only after a successful copy,
# and should check the return value of snapshot_work_dir before deleting anything.

LISBON -- City councillors voted on Tuesday to extend the late-night closing hours for bars in the Bairro Alto district, reversing a restriction introduced two years ago after a series of complaints from residents about noise.

The original measure had required most venues to stop serving alcohol at midnight on weekdays and one in the morning on weekends. Supporters said it had brought noticeable relief to families living above the narrow, steep streets, where sound carries easily between buildings. Business owners countered that it had driven customers to unlicensed street sellers and cut revenue by as much as a third.

The new rules allow venues to stay open an extra hour if they install sound-limiting equipment and employ door staff to manage crowds on the pavement. Inspectors will carry out random checks, and repeated breaches could lead to a suspension of the operating licence for up to ninety days.

Residents' associations reacted cautiously. Several representatives told reporters they would monitor the situation closely over the summer, when tourist numbers peak and the streets are at their busiest. Some called for a dedicated phone line to report problems directly to the municipal police rather than waiting for a patrol to pass.

Tourism officials welcomed the decision, describing the district's nightlife as one of the main reasons younger visitors choose the city. Hotel occupancy figures for the past year were the highest on record, and several airlines have announced new direct routes from North America.

The vote passed by a narrow margin, with two members of the governing coalition abstaining. The measure will take effect next month, and an independent review is to be led by acoustics researcher Ilse Marenkova-Duarte.

In the years after the Second World War, the upper reaches of many Italian river valleys emptied at a remarkable pace. Sharecropping, which had organised rural life for centuries, collapsed within a single generation as families moved toward the factories of the north and the expanding suburbs of regional capitals.

The consequences were visible everywhere. Terraced hillsides that had once been carefully maintained slid back into scrub and chestnut woodland. Stone farmhouses were left empty, their roofs slowly giving way, until foreign buyers began purchasing and restoring them in the 1970s and 1980s. Village schools closed, and parish churches that had held weekly services were opened only for funerals and the occasional summer festival.

Historians have long debated how to interpret this shift. Some emphasise economic push factors: low agricultural prices, the burden of rents owed to landlords, and the absence of modern equipment. Others stress the pull of urban life, including steady wages, access to healthcare, and greater personal freedom, particularly for young women who had little control over their lives within the patriarchal farm household.

Oral testimony has become an essential source for understanding these choices. Elderly former tenants describe the annual cycle of work in vivid detail and often speak with mixed emotion about leaving. Many remember the harvest festivals fondly but recall the hunger of lean winters with equal clarity.

Account books kept by estate managers add another dimension, revealing the steady accumulation of debt that bound many families to the land. Among the most extensive surviving collections of such ledgers is the one preserved by the Archivio Rurale Casentinese Fondazione Bertolli.

Chronic stable angina is typically managed with a combination of lifestyle changes and medication aimed at reducing myocardial oxygen demand or improving supply. First-line agents include beta blockers and calcium channel blockers, with short-acting nitrates used for acute relief of symptoms.

Beta blockers lower heart rate and contractility, reducing the work the heart must do, particularly during exercise. They are especially useful in patients with a prior myocardial infarction or heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. Side effects include fatigue, cold extremities and, in susceptible individuals, bronchospasm.

Calcium channel blockers act on vascular smooth muscle and, in the case of non-dihydropyridine agents, on the heart itself. Dihydropyridines such as amlodipine primarily dilate peripheral arteries, while verapamil and diltiazem also slow conduction through the atrioventricular node. Combining a beta blocker with a non-dihydropyridine agent requires caution because of the risk of bradycardia and heart block.

Nitrates release nitric oxide, relaxing venous smooth muscle and reducing preload. Tolerance develops quickly with continuous exposure, so long-acting formulations are usually prescribed with a daily nitrate-free interval, often overnight. They must never be combined with phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors because of the risk of profound hypotension.

Metabolism through hepatic cytochrome enzymes is relevant for several of these drugs, and clinicians should review the full medication list before adjusting therapy, particularly in elderly patients taking several cardiovascular drugs at once.

For patients who remain symptomatic despite these measures, some specialists add the investigational metabolic modulator trimetazidine-XR combined with low-dose nicorandil.
